categories.name: Core systems: health record and practice management
categories.summary: The electronic health record and the billing system (often sold together as a practice management system) that the practice runs on. The questions are fit, cost, and how much of what is already paid for is actually used.
good_looks_like: The systems fit how the practice works: office schedule, hospital rounds, facility census or home visits.
The practice uses the eligibility, automatic claim checking, remittance posting and reporting features it already pays for.
Total yearly cost per clinician is known, including add-on modules and per-claim fees.
Data can be exported in full without the vendor's help.
failure_modes: Staff work around a system built for a different kind of practice.
The practice pays for a second product to do what a switched-off feature of the first would do.
A system is replaced to fix a process problem, and the problem moves to the new system.
Nobody can produce a full export of charges, payments and adjustments.
key_questions: What does each system cost per clinician per year, all in?
Which features we pay for are not turned on?
Can we export every transaction with its dates and codes?
When does each contract renew, and what notice is required?

actions.action: List every system with cost and renewal date
actions.detail: Include per-claim, per-statement and add-on charges from a year of invoices.

actions.action: Ask the vendor for a feature review
actions.detail: Many vendors will walk through unused features at no charge. Ask the account manager for the list of modules on the contract.

Charges, payments, adjustments and patient balances, by service date. A certified health record must also let a user export all of a patient's stored record without the developer's help (45 CFR 170.315(b)(10)).

actions.action: Fix the process before replacing the system
actions.detail: Write down the failing step and try it with the current tools first.

categories.applies_when: Every practice. Clinicians who work in hospitals or nursing facilities often chart in the facility's record, so the practice's own system is mainly for billing and must handle census-based charge capture, several places of service and mobile use, which office-oriented products often do poorly.

vendor_refs.note: Adds a demonstration script built on exception cases and a 60-point vendor scorecard. Cites no sources, omits the federal data export rule, and calls clearinghouse rejections denials.
Argues for reconfiguring before replacing and gives an audit of claim edits. Wrongly treats denials of checked claims as proof the edits are misconfigured. Many denials no edit can catch.
Suggests a yearly list of every billing tool with its cost. Its keep-or-cancel test counts only staff hours saved, and its cost shares have no source.

categories.evidence_note: Management practice, plus one federal rule: certified health records must include a data export (45 CFR 170.315(b)(10)). Free cost figures from the Medical Group Management Association (MGMA) date from 2015 to 2022, use different definitions, and show rough scale only.

metrics.name: Technology cost per full-time clinician
metrics.definition: Yearly spending on software, hosting, clearinghouse, devices and technology support, per full-time clinician.
metrics.formula: Annual technology spending / number of full-time-equivalent clinicians
metrics.benchmark_note: MGMA's last free per-physician figures are old: $14,000 to $19,000 in technology operating expense (2016 data) and $32,500 including staff and equipment (2015). Its 2022 survey report put the median near $2 per total relative value unit. Use your own trend.
metrics.data_hint: A year of vendor invoices from the accounting system.
metrics.vendor_claim: Technology typically runs about 10% to 15% of total billing cost. Above 20% with no saving in staff time signals poor return.
metrics.vendor_verdict: Unverifiable. No source is given, the base is billing cost rather than clinicians, and it counts billing tools only.

categories.name: Integrations and data flow
categories.summary: How information moves between the health record, billing system, clearinghouse (the service that passes claims to payers), payers, bank, accounting and outside facilities. Every place a person retypes data is a place for delay and error.
good_looks_like: Eligibility, claims, claim status, remittances and deposits all move electronically for every payer that offers it.
Charges flow from the point of care to the billing system without retyping.
The practice has a simple diagram of what connects to what.
A failed transfer raises an alert the same day.
The practice has standing access to the records of the hospitals and facilities where its patients are seen, by portal, remote login or a health information exchange.
failure_modes: Remittances arrive on paper for a payer that offers them electronically.
A census or schedule is typed from one system into another, and names or dates drift.
An interface stops and nobody notices until claims are missing.
Accounting gets monthly totals by hand, so books and billing never agree.
A plan pays by virtual credit card, the practice pays a card fee on each payment, and nobody asks for bank transfer instead.
key_questions: For which payers do we still receive paper remittances or checks?
Where does anyone type the same information twice?
How would we know today if a data feed had stopped?
Do deposits in accounting tie to payments posted in billing?

actions.action: Enroll every payer for electronic remittance and deposit
actions.detail: Work down the payer list by dollars. Record enrollment dates. A health plan must use the standard electronic remittance and bank transfer when a practice asks, even if it now pays by virtual credit card (45 CFR 162.925).
Boxes for each system and arrows for each transfer, marked automatic or manual.

actions.action: Remove one manual re-entry point each quarter
actions.detail: Start with the one that touches the most claims.
A count of records received today against the usual number.

actions.action: Ask vendors about the 2027 payer interfaces
actions.detail: Medicare Advantage, Medicaid and federal marketplace plans must offer prior authorization and provider data interfaces, generally from January 1, 2027 (federal rule CMS-0057-F). Ask when your health record will connect.

categories.applies_when: Every practice. Facility-based practices also depend on getting the census, face sheets (the facility's page of patient and insurance details) and status changes from hospitals and nursing homes, usually through portals or reports that need a routine.

vendor_refs.note: Prompts the practice to ask its vendors about electronic prior authorization. Wrongly says payers must already offer it. The federal deadline is January 1, 2027, for certain plans only.
Admits the purchased workbooks connect to no health record, billing system or clearinghouse and need every figure typed in. An example of the re-entry this area warns about.

categories.evidence_note: A health plan's duty to use standard electronic transactions on request is federal regulation. Labor cost per transaction is measured each year by CAQH, an industry group that surveys health plans and providers. Which connections to build first is judgment.

metrics.name: Places where data is entered by hand a second time
metrics.definition: Count of steps where a person retypes information that already exists in another system.
metrics.benchmark_note: No benchmark for the count. Why count: CAQH's 2025 Index put a medical provider's average cost at $8.03 per manual transaction against $2.65 electronic. Its 2024 Index (2023 data) showed eligibility at $8.57 against $2.00 and claim status at $13.80 against $3.64.
metrics.data_hint: The data-flow diagram, reviewed with the people who do the work.

categories.name: Analytics, dashboards and the data model
categories.summary: One trusted place where the practice's numbers live, with agreed definitions, so that a measure means the same thing every month and can be traced back to the claims behind it.
good_looks_like: Billing, bank and accounting data land in one store on a schedule.
Each measure has a written definition and formula.
The scorecard is produced automatically and shows the date of the data.
Any number can be opened to see the records behind it.
failure_modes: The billing system, the accountant and the owner's spreadsheet give three different collection totals.
A measure changes because someone changed the report filter, not because performance changed.
Reports are built by hand each month, so they arrive late or not at all.
Dashboards show totals with no way to see which claims make them up.
key_questions: Do our billing reports and our bank deposits agree for last month?
Is each scorecard measure defined in writing?
How many scorecard numbers are typed in by hand?
Can we list the claims behind any figure?

actions.action: Write a definition for every measure
actions.detail: Name, formula, source table, and what is included and excluded.

actions.action: Load source data on a schedule
actions.detail: Daily or more often for billing data, monthly for accounting.
Payments posted against deposits against the income statement.
Every summary should link to its rows.

categories.applies_when: Every practice, at a scale that fits: a two-clinician practice may need only a monthly export and a spreadsheet with fixed definitions, while one with automation can keep a small database. A practice that uses a billing company should still hold its own copy of the data.

vendor_refs.note: Good test: have the vendor run denial rate by payer, days in receivables and net collection rate live. Treats first-pass acceptance and clean claim rate as one measure.
Right that a practice should keep its own access to billing data and recompute a billing company's figures. Its own definition of days in receivables is non-standard.

categories.evidence_note: Standard definitions exist: the 29 MAP Keys of the Healthcare Financial Management Association (HFMA) and the DataDive glossary of the Medical Group Management Association (MGMA). Adopt them where they fit. HFMA defines measures but sets no targets. No benchmark exists for analytics itself.

metrics.name: Scorecard measures produced automatically
metrics.definition: Share of the practice's scorecard measures that are calculated from source data without anyone typing a number.
metrics.formula: Measures calculated automatically / measures on the scorecard x 100
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. Automation matters less than a fixed definition, so define first and automate second.
metrics.data_hint: The scorecard's own list of measures and sources.

metrics.name: Hours from an event to its appearance in reports
metrics.definition: Time between something happening, such as a payment posting, and that fact showing in the practice's reports.
metrics.formula: Time a fact first appears in the reports - time the event happened, in hours. Use the median of a small sample
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. Daily refresh is enough for most management decisions. Work queues need same-day data.
metrics.data_hint: Load logs or the timestamp on each report, compared with posting times in the billing system.

categories.name: Automation and AI agents
categories.summary: Using rules engines, scheduled routines and artificial intelligence (AI) agents to do clerical billing work: checking coverage, entering charges, posting payments, following up claims and producing reports.
good_looks_like: Automation is applied first to high-volume clerical steps with clear rules.
Each automated step has a written rule, a log of what it did, and a person who owns it.
Results are measured before and after: cost, speed and error rate.
Tasks that change what is billed stay with a qualified person.
failure_modes: A tool is bought before the process is understood, and automates the confusion.
Automation quietly resubmits or writes off claims and nobody reviews the pattern.
Savings are claimed from a vendor's slide, never measured.
The one person who understood the automation leaves.
key_questions: Which steps do we repeat hundreds of times a month by the same rule?
For each automated step, where is the rule written and where is the log?
What did automation change in cost to collect and days in receivables?
Who can turn it off, and who would notice if it stopped?

actions.action: Rank tasks by volume and rule clarity
actions.detail: Eligibility checks, charge entry from a feed, remittance posting and claim status are the usual first candidates.

actions.action: Write the rule before automating it
actions.detail: A plain-language rule a new employee could follow, approved by the owner.
What, when, on which claim, under which rule.
Cost to collect, days to submit, first-pass payment and corrections, for three months each side.

categories.applies_when: Any practice with repetitive clerical volume: the smaller the staff, the larger the relative gain and the dependence on whoever built it. Practices with no front desk gain most from automated coverage checks and census-to-charge matching, because nobody sees the patient's insurance card.

vendor_refs.note: Sound priority: automate steps that prevent rework, such as coverage checks and charge capture. Its automatic write-off of small balances ignores the rule against routine waiver of Medicare cost sharing.
Points to a feature many systems have: routing denials to work lists by reason code. Says almost nobody uses it and results show in 30 days, with no data.

categories.evidence_note: Savings from electronic transactions are measured each year by CAQH, an industry group whose 2025 Index found about one-quarter of providers using AI, mostly for administrative tasks. Evidence on AI agents in billing is early and mostly from vendors, so measure your own results.

metrics.name: Routine transactions completed without human work
metrics.definition: Share of a defined set of routine transactions, such as eligibility checks, charge entries or payment postings, completed by automation with no manual step.
metrics.formula: Transactions completed automatically / transactions of that type x 100
metrics.benchmark_note: No benchmark for a practice's own automation rate was found. Nearest public figure: CAQH's 2025 Index shows the share handled fully electronically at medical plans, 96% for eligibility checks, 81% for claim status and 40% for prior authorization. Track by transaction type.
metrics.data_hint: Automation run logs and billing system user fields.

metrics.name: Automated actions later corrected or reversed
metrics.definition: Share of automated actions that a person or a payer later had to correct, reverse or redo.
metrics.formula: Automated actions corrected or reversed / automated actions x 100
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. This is the main safety measure for automated billing. Set an alert level from your own first three months.
metrics.data_hint: A monthly sample review plus reversal and void reports.

categories.name: Controls for automation and AI
categories.summary: The rules that keep billing work done by software or artificial intelligence (AI) safe: what it may do alone, what needs a person, how actions are logged and tested, and who answers for errors. The practice is responsible for every claim, however it was prepared.
good_looks_like: A written policy lists which actions automation may take alone and which need approval.
Any change to a code, modifier, diagnosis, date, place of service or rendering clinician is approved by a qualified person and tied to the record.
A fixed sample of automated actions is reviewed against the charts every month.
New or changed rules are tested on a copy before they touch live claims.
failure_modes: An AI agent changes a code or modifier to get past a payer's claim check and resubmits, with no one checking the note.
One wrong rule repeats across hundreds of claims before anyone looks.
Documentation drafted by an AI scribe is signed in bulk without being read.
Patient data is sent to an AI tool whose vendor has signed no business associate agreement, which the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) requires first (45 CFR 164.502(e)).
Software is set so the higher-paid code is always billed. A wound-care group agreed to pay $45 million in 2025 over allegations that included this.
key_questions: Which automated actions can change what is billed, and who approves each?
When did a person last sample automated actions against the charts?
Does every vendor or AI tool that sees patient data have a signed business associate agreement?
Do clinicians read and sign AI-drafted notes individually?

actions.detail: Clerical fixes may run alone. Anything that changes what is billed needs logged human approval. Medicare's electronic billing agreement holds the practice responsible for claims sent by its employees or agents (Claims Processing Manual, chapter 24, section 30.2).
A fixed number, chosen at random, compared with the source record, including the hospital's or facility's chart where the note lives. Record the result.
Run on a copy or a small batch and review the output.

actions.action: Have a coder review the rulebook yearly
actions.detail: An independent certified coder reads every rule that touches codes, dates or balances.

actions.action: Require individual sign-off on AI-drafted notes
actions.detail: Medicare requires the practitioner's signature on a note captured by AI, as confirmation that it adequately documents the care (Program Integrity Manual, chapter 3, section 3.3.2.4).

categories.applies_when: Any practice using automation, AI scribes or AI agents in documentation or billing, including when a billing company or software vendor runs the automation. State law can say the same: in Florida, the Medicaid statute makes the provider responsible for preparing and submitting each claim (section 409.913).

vendor_refs.note: Shows simple change control: a revision log kept before release and a rule separating minor from major changes. Reports no testing of the changed workbooks.
Like 22 other documents, carries one line saying AI-generated drafts need review by a qualified person. The library gives no policy, log or sampling method for automated billing.

categories.evidence_note: Reckless disregard suffices for false claims liability (31 U.S.C. 3729), Medicare's billing agreement makes the practice answerable for its agents' claims, and practitioners must sign AI-captured notes. No federal guidance on AI claim correction was found. Enforcers named health record manipulation a priority in 2025.

metrics.name: High-risk automated actions with documented human review
metrics.definition: Share of automated actions that change what is billed, or write off a balance, that carry a logged approval by a qualified person.
metrics.formula: High-risk automated actions with logged approval / high-risk automated actions x 100
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. The target from first principles is 100% for any change to code, modifier, diagnosis, date, place of service or clinician.
metrics.data_hint: The automation log joined to the approval record.

categories.name: Cybersecurity
categories.summary: Protecting systems and patient data from loss, theft and ransomware. Small practices are targeted too and can suffer proportionally greater damage. The 2024 clearinghouse attack that disrupted claims nationwide began with stolen sign-in details used on a portal without multi-factor sign-in.
good_looks_like: Every account that can reach patient data or money uses multi-factor sign-in, meaning a password plus a second proof such as a phone code.
Each person has their own account, which the Security Rule of the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) requires (45 CFR 164.312), with only the access the job needs.
Devices are encrypted, patched and able to be wiped if lost.
There is a written plan for a breach or ransomware event, and the cyber insurer's phone number is on it.
Staff are trained to spot fake email, and the email system filters and flags messages from outside senders.
failure_modes: A shared password for the billing system or the bank.
A former employee's or vendor's access is still active a year later.
An access key or password is pasted into an email or chat.
Backups exist but were never tested, or sit on the same network the attacker encrypted.
key_questions: Is multi-factor sign-in on for email, billing, the bank and remote access?
Who has administrator rights, and do they need them?
When were accounts of departed staff and vendors removed?
Do we know what to do in the first hour of a ransomware attack?

actions.detail: Email, health record, billing, bank, payroll, cloud storage and remote access.

actions.action: Remove unused accounts and rotate exposed keys
actions.detail: Review all users and access keys, the passwords that software uses to reach other systems. Replace any that was ever pasted into a message.
Automatic updates on, disk encryption on, remote wipe for phones and laptops.

Who to call, how to isolate systems, how to keep billing going, the insurer's hotline, and the HIPAA duty to tell patients whose data was exposed no later than 60 days after discovery (45 CFR 164.404).

HIPAA requires one but sets no interval (45 CFR 164.308(a)(1)). The free federal Security Risk Assessment Tool guides a small practice through it, though using it does not prove compliance. Redo it yearly and when systems change.

categories.applies_when: Every practice: those using cloud systems and automated tools have fewer servers to protect but more accounts and access keys to control. Clinicians who work in hospitals and facilities carry patient data on phones and laptops, so device controls matter more.

vendor_refs.note: Sound focus on shared logins, role-based access and vendor agreements. Wrongly says current guidance requires a yearly risk analysis and that unencrypted email always breaks the Security Rule.

categories.evidence_note: HIPAA rules require a risk analysis, unique user accounts and breach notice and leave most other specifics to the practice. The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) publishes voluntary goals. A 2025 proposal requiring multi-factor sign-in was not final as of November 2026.

metrics.name: Accounts protected by multi-factor sign-in
metrics.definition: Share of user accounts with access to patient data or money that require a second factor to sign in.
metrics.formula: Accounts with multi-factor sign-in enforced / accounts with such access x 100
metrics.benchmark_note: No measured benchmark was found. The target from first principles is 100%. HHS lists multi-factor sign-in among its essential, voluntary cybersecurity goals for health care (2024), and the 2025 proposed Security Rule would require it. Compare with your own trend.
metrics.data_hint: The user list in each system's administration settings.

categories.name: Technology vendor selection and management
categories.summary: Choosing, contracting with and reviewing the companies whose software the practice depends on. The contract decides who owns the data, what happens when things fail, and how the practice can leave.
good_looks_like: Needs are written down before any demonstration is watched.
References are called, and they are practices of similar size and type.
Contracts state price increases, service levels, data ownership, export on exit and a business associate agreement, the privacy contract federal law requires of any vendor that handles patient data.
Each critical vendor gets a yearly review of cost, performance and security.
failure_modes: A purchase follows an impressive demonstration of features the practice never uses.
The contract renews automatically for three years with a price increase.
On leaving, the vendor charges for the practice's own data or delivers it in an unusable form.
A vendor handles patient data with no signed agreement.
key_questions: For each critical vendor, when does the contract renew and what notice is needed?
Does each contract say we own our data and can export it?
Which vendors that see patient data lack a signed business associate agreement?
Where does each vendor store our data?

actions.detail: Name, purpose, yearly cost, renewal date, notice period, agreement on file, where data is stored.
Ten things the system must do for this practice, ranked.

Agree export format, cost and timing in writing. Charging for the standard export when you switch systems, or a conversion fee not agreed in writing at purchase, can be information blocking by a certified health record developer (45 CFR 171.302).
Cost against budget, outages, support quality, security attestations, and a check of the federal exclusion list for billing and staffing contractors.

categories.applies_when: Every practice. State law can add requirements: Florida, for example, requires providers that use certified electronic health record technology to keep patient information stored offsite or in the cloud within the continental United States, its territories or Canada (section 408.051).

vendor_refs.note: Useful list of ten contract clauses that favor vendors and a 90-day evaluation plan. Its 180-day renewal notice advice is ambiguous. Omits business associate terms and federal export rules.
For billing companies: write data ownership into the contract, with full data handed over 30 days after notice of termination. Its fee ranges and performance floors cite no source.
Lists required business associate contract terms and a yearly review. Wrongly ties return or destruction of data to a breach. The rule ties it to the end of the contract.
Shows why update terms matter: the purchase covers one version only and excludes future updates and new editions.

categories.evidence_note: Business associate agreements and their required terms are federal regulation (45 CFR 164.308(b) and 164.504(e)). Data-location rules are state law. Selection and monitoring steps follow voluntary federal guidance for small health care organizations and general contract practice.

metrics.name: Critical vendors reviewed in the last 12 months
metrics.definition: Share of vendors the practice could not operate without that have had a documented review of cost, performance, contract terms and security within a year.
metrics.formula: Critical vendors reviewed in the last 12 months / critical vendors x 100
metrics.benchmark_note: No measured benchmark was found. The first-principles target is every critical vendor, once a year. Federal guidance for small practices suggests quarterly or twice-yearly reviews of an outsourced technology provider, and the 2025 proposed Security Rule would require yearly written security verification.
metrics.vendor_claim: Judge each new technology vendor against written benchmarks at 6, 12 and 24 months after signing.
metrics.vendor_verdict: Unverifiable. A sensible schedule with no source behind it. No public benchmark exists, so the yearly target here is set from first principles.

categories.name: Business continuity and disaster recovery
categories.summary: Keeping care and billing going when a system, a vendor, a building or a key person is unavailable. Two months after the 2024 clearinghouse attack, three-quarters of respondents to an informal American Medical Association survey still had trouble submitting claims.
good_looks_like: Backups of critical data are made automatically, stored separately, and restored in a test at least yearly.
A one-page downtime plan covers loss of the health record, the billing system, the clearinghouse and the office.
The practice has a second route for claims or a line of credit for an outage.
Written procedures let a second person run each critical task.
failure_modes: Backups prove unusable on the day they are needed. In a 2026 Medical Group Management Association poll, 19% of leaders were very confident of recovering quickly from a cyberattack.
A clearinghouse outage stops all claims and there is no alternative route and no cash cushion.
Everything depends on one person's laptop or one person's memory.
A storm closes the office and nobody can reach schedules or phone lists.
key_questions: When did we last restore a backup as a test?
If our clearinghouse were down for three weeks, how would we submit claims and meet payroll?
Could someone else run billing next week with the written procedures?
Where is the plan kept, and can we reach it without our own systems?
Has our billing system vendor confirmed it can route claims through a second clearinghouse?

actions.detail: Restore a sample of records to a separate place and confirm they are readable.
For each critical system: how to work without it, who to call, and how to catch up.

actions.action: Arrange a fallback for claims and cash
actions.detail: A second clearinghouse connection or payer portals, and an unused credit line. In 2024 Medicare's relief was an advance of up to 30 days of payments, recovered from later claims over 90 days.
Step-by-step notes for payroll, claim submission, payment posting and credentialing.

categories.applies_when: Every practice: cloud systems reduce the risk of losing data but increase dependence on vendors and internet access. Practices that work in hospitals and nursing facilities also depend on those facilities' systems and should know their downtime procedures for notes and orders.

vendor_refs.note: Good questions for vendors: downtime hours and longest outage last year, and what an uptime promise excludes. Nothing on backups, restore tests or a clearinghouse outage.
Treats continuity only as a planned change of billing company, with a 90-day exit plan. Does not cover a sudden loss of the vendor.

categories.evidence_note: The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) Security Rule requires a contingency plan with backup and disaster recovery (45 CFR 164.308(a)(7)) and leaves test frequency to the practice. A 2025 proposal would require yearly plan tests and monthly test restores. Fallback advice is judgment.

metrics.name: Months since a backup restore was tested
metrics.definition: Time since the practice last restored data from backup as a test and confirmed it was usable.
metrics.formula: Today - date of the last successful restore test, in months
metrics.benchmark_note: No measured benchmark was found. A reasonable floor is a test restore at least once a year and after any change of backup method. The 2025 proposed Security Rule, not final, would require monthly test restores and recovery of critical systems within 72 hours.

categories.name: Data governance and records
categories.summary: Who may see and change which data, how long records are kept, and who is responsible for their accuracy. It covers medical records, billing records and the procedures that describe how the practice works.
good_looks_like: A written retention schedule covers medical, billing and business records, using the longest period that applies, which is often 10 years for a practice with Medicare Advantage contracts.
User access is reviewed on a schedule and removed the day someone leaves.
One person is responsible for the accuracy of each key data set.
Patient details are kept out of systems that have no agreement to hold them.
failure_modes: Records are destroyed too early for an audit, or kept forever with no plan.
Access accumulates: people keep rights from roles they left years ago.
Patient details end up in personal email, text messages, chat, a shared drive or an artificial intelligence tool with no agreement to hold them.
Nobody owns the payer list or the fee schedule, so both drift.
A clinician's notes live only in a hospital's or nursing home's record, and the practice cannot produce them when an auditor asks years later.
key_questions: How long do we keep medical records, billing records and remittances, and why?
When did we last review who has access to each system?
Where could patient details be sitting outside the health record and billing system?
Who owns the payer list, the fee schedule and the provider enrollment records?

actions.detail: List record types with the governing rule. Medicare requires 7 years for orders and referrals (42 CFR 424.516), Medicare Advantage plans require 10 (42 CFR 422.504), and state law sets the medical record minimum.

actions.action: Review who has access to each system
actions.detail: Print the user list for each system and confirm each person and role. Quarterly suits a small practice. Six months is the outer limit. Also do it whenever someone leaves.

actions.action: Keep patient details out of unapproved tools
actions.detail: Name the approved tools in writing and train staff. Where files are exported or shared by software, add an automatic check that blocks patient identifiers.

actions.action: Assign an owner to each key data set
actions.detail: Payer list, fee schedule, provider enrollments, facility list.

categories.applies_when: Every practice. Retention periods come from state medical record law, Medicare rules and payer contracts, so the schedule differs by state and payer mix: in Florida, for example, physicians must keep records at least five years from the last patient contact (Rule 64B8-10.002) and Medicaid records five years from the service (section 409.913).

vendor_refs.note: Covers role-based access, individual logins and removing departed staff. Overstates one rule: says minimum necessary can only be met by system lock-out, where the regulation asks for reasonable efforts.

Gives state retention periods (its Florida entry is right) and the 10-year Medicare Advantage rule. Wrongly bases a six-year Medicare claim-record rule on 45 CFR 164.316, which covers security documents.

categories.evidence_note: Retention periods are regulation and contract: 7 years for Medicare orders and referrals, 10 years under Medicare Advantage contracts, 6 years for federal security policy documents, and state law for medical records. The six-year overpayment lookback is regulation. Access review frequency is judgment.

metrics.name: Months since user access was reviewed
metrics.definition: Time since the practice last reviewed the list of users and access rights for each system that holds patient data or money.
metrics.formula: Today - date of the last documented access review, in months
metrics.benchmark_note: No measured benchmark exists. The federal Security Rule expects access rights to be reviewed but sets no interval (45 CFR 164.308(a)(4)). A reasonable standard is every three to six months and at each departure. A 2025 proposal would end access within an hour of departure.
metrics.vendor_claim: Check access settings and logins in a yearly self-audit, and review system activity logs every quarter.
metrics.vendor_verdict: Partly supported. The Security Rule requires regular review of system activity and expects review of access rights, but names no interval. Both frequencies are the vendor's choice.
